html:
A stone inscription of 1113 at Bagan in Myanmar that gives the same text in four languages: Pyu, Mon, Old Burmese and Pali. It did for the lost Pyu language what the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian.

It tells how Prince Yazakumar, son of King Kyansittha of Pagan, built a temple and a gold Buddha image for his dying father, and gave it three villages that had come to him from the king. The text survives on two pillars that are nearly identical. Its Burmese version is one of the oldest known texts in that language.

The four languages show who mattered at Pagan. Pyu was the language of the old Pyu city-states, already fading. Mon was the language of the southern neighbours whose monks and scribes had shaped Pagan after the adoption of Theravada Buddhism. Pali was the language of scripture, and Burmese was rising. With the Pali and Mon versions as a key, scholars in the early 20th century were able to work out the Pyu script.
sum: A stone inscription of 1113 at Bagan in Myanmar that gives the same text in four languages: Pyu, Mon, Old Burmese and Pali. It did for the lost Pyu language what the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian.
